newsitem.title: CHINA: China says need ideological breakthrough to reform.
newsitem.headline: China says need ideological breakthrough to reform.

text.p: One of China's propaganda tsars said its far-reaching reforms could regress without an ideological breakthrough in a raging debate over "socialism" versus "capitalism".

"Reforms...have entered a crucial period in which success or failure will be determined at one stroke," Li Junru, deputy director of the theoretical department of the Communist Party's Propaganda Department, said in an interview published in the China Economic Times on Tuesday.
"If there is no breakthrough in progress, retrogression could be a possibility," Li said. "The fruit of reform could be destroyed in one moment. Serious, unthinkable problems could appear."

In recent months, die-hard Marxists have intensified attacks on the capitalist-style reforms of late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, rekindling a debate on whether China should embrace un-Marxist concepts such as free markets, private enterprise and stock exchanges.
However, the communist propaganda official said an ideological breakthrough was needed in the raging debate over "public" versus "private" to push through with more reforms.
"We must boldly...learn and borrow...methods used by capitalist countries to achieve modernisation," Li said.

Li blasted leftism as an "outdated concept from an old system" that should make way for policies "in the interest of productivity, in the interest of boosting overall national strength and in the interest of improving the lives of the people".
Deng abandoned Soviet-style central planning and embraced market reform in the late 1970s to revive the stagnant economy.

Deng dubbed the changes "socialism with Chinese characteristics" -- an ideological sleight of hand that enabled him to push through changes seen by leftists, or orthodox Marxists, as ideologically incorrect.
Communist Party boss and state president Jiang Zemin has called for vigilance against leftism before a crucial five-yearly party congress in September or October.
Jiang was expected to win a vote of confidence at the congress for his reforms aimed at trimming the state sector and reviving private industry, analysts said.
Li called for efforts to co-opt comrades with different views on reform, instead of the past practice of purging them.

Party reformers and hard-liners have been jostling for position in the run-up to the five-yearly congress that will set the path of the world's most populous nation and elect the leaders who will govern it into the 21st century.
Party leaders have been holding their annual summer gathering at the seaside resort of Beidaihe, where much of the groundwork for the congress is being laid.
Li said reforms were needed if China were to stave off challenges from Russia, Eastern Europe and the Central Asian republics that have turned their backs on communism.
"Once their reforms take a turn for the better...our unshakeable faith in socialism could suffer a lashing," Li said.
Russia's economy had been in shambles after the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, but began to grow in July for the first time since the disintegration of the communist giant.
